The study conducted in Dakar, Senegal, focused on the age distribution of patients attending primary care clinics and was published in Tropical Medicine and International Health in 2018 (Volume 23, Issue 5, Pages 541-548). 2. Bhatla et al. investigated the association between Chlamydia trachomatis infection and human papillomavirus (HPV) as well as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in a pilot study. This research was published in the Indian Journal of Medical Research in 2013 (Volume 137, Issue 3, Pages 533-539). 3. Bristow et al. explored the etiology of vaginal symptoms in rural Haiti, with findings published in the International Journal of STD and AIDS in 2014 (Volume 25, Issue 9, Pages 669-675). 4. Cai et al. examined the relationship between genital Chlamydia trachomatis infection and poor sexual quality of life in young, sexually active women. Their findings were published in the Journal of Sexual Medicine in 2011 (Volume 8, Issue 4, Pages 1131-1137). 5. Chirenje et al. studied the etiology of vaginal discharge syndrome in Zimbabwe as part of the Zimbabwe STI Etiology Study. The results were published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2018 (Volume 45, Issue 6, Pages 422-428). 6. Corbeto et al. analyzed the epidemiological features and determinants of Chlamydia trachomatis infection among women in Catalonia, Spain. This study appeared in the International Journal of STD and AIDS in 2010 (Volume 21, Issue 10, Pages 718-722). 7. De Jongh et al. assessed the risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in women attending a termination of pregnancy clinic in Pretoria, South Africa. Their findings were published in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology in 2010 (Volume 30, Issue 5, Pages 480-483). 8. De Lima et al. investigated sexually transmitted bacterial infections among young women in central-western Brazil, with results published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2014 (Volume 25, Pages 16-21). 9. Dela et al. identified risk factors associated with gonorrhea and chlamydia transmission in selected health facilities in Ghana. This study was published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2019 (Volume 19, Article 425). 10. Fonck et al. evaluated the validity of the vaginal discharge algorithm among pregnant and non-pregnant women in Nairobi, Kenya. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2000 (Volume 76, Issue 1, Pages 33-38). 11. Garcia et al. studied sexually transmitted and reproductive tract infections in symptomatic clients of pharmacies in Lima, Peru. The results were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2007 (Volume 83, Issue 2, Pages 142-146). 12. Geisler et al. examined pelvic examination findings and Chlamydia trachomatis infection in asymptomatic young women screened using nucleic acid amplification tests. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2007 (Volume 34, Issue 6, Pages 335-338). 13. Goldzier et al. investigated the relationship between chlamydial infection and unplanned pregnancy in women with ready access to healthcare. Their findings were published in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2001 (Volume 98, Issue 6, Pages 1117-1123). 14. Goyal et al. reported on the prevalence of Trichomonas vaginalis infection in symptomatic adolescent females presenting to a pediatric emergency department. This study was published in Academic Emergency Medicine in 2011 (Volume 18, Issue 7, Pages 763-766). 15. Guimaraes et al. evaluated the utility of risk scores and gynecological examinations for screening sexually transmitted infections in sexually active adolescents. Their findings were published in BMC Medicine in 2009 (Volume 7, Article 8). 16. Hoque et al. detected Chlamydia trachomatis using immunological and genetic methods in female sex workers and the local female population of reproductive age in Mymensingh, Bangladesh. This study was published in the Japanese Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2013 (Volume 66, Issue 3, Pages 256-259). 17. Huppert et al. investigated urinary tract infections and Chlamydia trachomatis infections in adolescent females. Their findings were published in the Journal of Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology in 2003 (Volume 16, Issue 3, Pages 133-137). 18. Huppert et al. also studied the detection of Mycoplasma genitalium using transcription-mediated amplification and its association with Chlamydia trachomatis in adolescent women. This research was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2008 (Volume 35, Issue 3, Pages 250-254). 19. Ikeme et al. reported on the seroprevalence of Chlamydia trachomatis in Enugu, Nigeria. Their findings were published in the Nigerian Journal of Clinical Practice in 2011 (Volume 14, Issue 2, Pages 176-180). 20. Imai et al. studied the prevalence and risk factors of asymptomatic chlamydial infection among students in Japan. This research was published in the International Journal of STD and AIDS in 2004 (Volume 15, Issue 6, Pages 408-414). 21. Imai et al. also conducted a population-based study on asymptomatic Chlamydia trachomatis infection among male and female students. Their findings were published in the International Journal of STD and AIDS in 2010 (Volume 21, Issue 5, Pages 362-366). 22. Kufa et al. examined the demographic and clinical profiles of women presenting with vaginal discharge syndrome at primary care facilities in South Africa, with implications for management. This study was published in the South African Medical Journal in 2018 (Volume 108, Issue 10). 23. Landers et al. evaluated the predictive value of clinical diagnosis for lower genital tract infections in women. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2004 (Volume 190, Issue 4, Pages 1004-1010). 24. Lewis et al. analyzed trends and associations of Trichomonas vaginalis infection in men and women with genital discharge syndromes in Johannesburg, South Africa. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2013 (Volume 89, Issue 6, Pages 523-527). 25. Lubbad et al. investigated bacterial, viral, and fungal genital tract infections in pregnant women in Gaza, Palestine. Their findings were published in the West African Journal of Medicine in 2007 (Volume 26, Issue 2, Pages 138-142). 26. Mania-Pramanik et al. studied the use of vaginal pH in diagnosing infections and its association with reproductive manifestations. This research was published in the Journal of Clinical Laboratory Analysis in 2008 (Volume 22, Issue 5, Pages 375-379). 27. Marconi et al. examined chlamydial infection in a high-risk population and its association with vaginal flora patterns. Their findings were published in the Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics in 2012 (Volume 285, Issue 4, Pages 1013-1018). 28. Mbizvo et al. identified determinants of reproductive tract infections among asymptomatic women in Harare, Zimbabwe. This study was published in the Central African Journal of Medicine in 2001 (Volume 47, Issue 3, Pages 57-64). 29. Molaei et al. reported on the frequency of gonorrheal and chlamydial infections in Zanjanian women during 2013-2014. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Reproductive BioMedicine in 2017 (Volume 15, Issue 2, Pages 75-82). 30. Mossong et al. conducted screening for Chlamydia trachomatis in secondary schools, family planning, and occupational health centers in Luxembourg. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2009 (Volume 85, Issue 6, Pages 455-458).
